newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia premier takes more duties, Yeltsin defiant.
newsitem.headline: Russia premier takes more duties, Yeltsin defiant.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, irritated by charges that Russia is drifting rudderless during his prolonged spell in hospital, has rounded on his many critics and insisted he was still at the helm of the vast country.

However in a sign of his much-reduced workload ahead of heart surgery later this year, Yeltsin's constitutional stand-in, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, began assuming more responsibilities on Friday to avert a possible power vacuum.

A pivotal figure in moves to seek influence during Yeltsin's absence, Chernomyrdin was due to chair the first meeting of Russia's new defence council, called to review the crucial issue of funding for the cash-strapped armed forces.
The premier was then expected to fly to the Kazakh capital Almaty to represent Russia in urgently convened security talks with the heads of several other ex-Soviet republics.
In a radio address on Thursday Yeltsin said it was too early to write him off and take his picture down from office walls.

"I am in touch with what is going on in the country. I am helped by a strong team of professionals," said Yeltsin, who has been in Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital since September 13 and faces a bypass operation in six to 10 weeks.
In recent days Communist Party chief Gennady Zyuganov has spearheaded opposition calls for Yeltsin to resign, saying his illness had paralysed decision-making.
But Yeltsin was defiant. "Don't rush to change the portraits. The country has a president and an active president at that," he said.

Yeltsin had his first meeting with national security chief Alexander Lebed in more than two months and ordered the outspoken ex-paratroop general to work more amicably with Chernomyrdin and the government team.
In a television appearance Yeltsin said he had dismissed a threat by Lebed to resign over a minor matter.
"He (Lebed) needs to get down to business now, carry out the tasks he already has and make more effort to work with the premier and with the other services," Yeltsin said.
"You can't quarrel with everyone all the time. You can't settle issues that way. Our state apparatus must live in peace."
Chernomyrdin and Lebed later sat down together with Chechen separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev for talks on the future of the breakaway region.
They agreed to set up a new joint body to rebuild Chechnya's war-ravaged economy and organise local elections, in line with a peace deal clinched by Lebed on August 31.

Lebed's peace agreement had been denounced on Wednesday in the State Duma lower chamber of parliament as a humiliating capitulation to the separatists that could lead to the disintegration of the Russian Federation.
But Yeltsin praised the deal for bringing a halt to 21 months of bloodshed in Chechnya, though he and Chernomyrdin both cautioned that much hard work remained to be done.

Yeltsin said in his radio address that he was "very worried" about the situation in the army, where many soldiers have not been paid for months. He urged the defence council, which includes top government ministers and security officials, to take concrete decisions during its meeting.
Yeltsin's words followed a warning from Lebed that the army was on the brink of mutiny.

Lebed has also sounded the alarm over the rise to power of the hardline Islamic Taleban militia in Afghanistan, the issue to be discussed in Almaty by Chernomyrdin and leaders of four other Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS).
The summit reflects Moscow's concern that the Taleban's drive to extend their control over Afghanistan could destabilise Tajikistan and other ex-Soviet republics in Central Asia.

Russia regards the southern flank of the CIS, a loose grouping erected on the ashes of the former Soviet Union, as its strategic underbelly and Russian border guards patrol Tajikistan's 1,500-km (900-mile) frontier with Afghanistan.
Lebed, a veteran of the Soviet Afghan war, said Russia should render all necessary help to the Afghan government driven out of Kabul last week.
